Towards the evolution of the new summer girl three conspicuous Americans have materially contributed. Probably the finest outfits made in Paris this season have been provided for Lady Curzon, Vicereine of India, to wear at the summer resort of Simla, and for Miss Sloane and Miss Fair, the two Vanderbilt brides. The personal tastes of all three of these women run to extremely slender effects, and their wardrobes, exemplifying great length of skirt and, in the case of two, the daringly decollete, have done much to establish and confirm the present modes.


A Chicago woman now married abroad who left Paris to accompany Lady Curzon to India, has written to American friends descriptions of several of the Vicereine's Simla dresses, all with clinging overskirts, transparent petticoats and, in case of the evening dresses, bodices which are nothing but broad waistbands with a wisp of lace draped over the corsage.


One of the most remarkable of these dresses is a costume of white India gauze. The foundation of this dress is pink silk, showing delicately through the trailing clouds of the lighter material. The gauze skirt is made with a series of flounces powdered with gold and caught in places by pink gauze rosettes. Over this comes a long redingote of Venetian point lace, which fits the figure more smoothly without wrinkles by some material like featherbone. The corsage is cut very low and round leaving the shoulders entirely bare, and being kept up only by strings of large pearls. The decolletage is edged by a bounce of gold-powdered gauze, which is continued in little fan-like frills crossing the arms some six inches below the shoulders. Nobody alludes to these frills as sleeves.


Following such light example, the summer girl will wear trailing skirt without a seam in the back; and, next its peculiar outline, one of the most notable things about her toilette will be its lavish use of exquisitely light and subtle wreaths and flower sprays.


A graceful evening dress for a young girl is carried out in white embroidered gauze hung over an underskirt of pink chiffon falling in many small, soft frills. The whole effect of the toilette is of great delicacy with gauze corsage falling quaintly away from the pink chiffon ruffles which frame the shoulders. Tiny gauze sleeves drop off the shoulders, leaving the task of supporting the bodice to trails of wild roses which are thrown over the shoulders. At the back of the bodice starts another rose spray, winding about the left side of the skirt to the front and thence dropping to the edge of the tunic, which it nearly encircles.


Another flower gown is of ivory Brussels net embroidered with a light running pattern of silver thread, sequins and tiny diamond dew drops. The hem of the skirt has an application of Brussels lace, giving a pretty broken edge, which falls over an under-robe of palest green chiffon; this reveals itself through the net as well as at the foot of the robe in a multitude of cloudy frills. The bodice of jewelled net and chiffon droops from the shoulders in Victorian style and has mitt sleeves of their entire length, and laced across with green velvet ribbon. A long garland of water lilies starting from the left shoulder falls to the back of the waist, and is brought around in front, where it is used to catch up the tunic, which is draped high on one side.


The summer girl is including Empire dresses in her wardrobe, the most successful of these having no tunics. One is of pale blue crepe de chine over whose surface plays an old silver light, is lightly embroidered half way up the skirt with small silver paillettes forming vine sprays with long tendrils. Lower down comes a wide insertion of the same embroidery giving a hint of an under-robe of white flushed with pink. The sleeves are lattices of pearls.


Simpler dresses are made of spangled or spotted nets over plain net or over chiffon. Delicate, cloudy grey nets are much in favor, usually with some touch of bright color. A clever girl can spangle her own dress with few evenings' labor, and with the pattern will be less elaborate than on those supplied by the shops, the glittering particles will stay on better and the effect will be even more desirable for the less formal festivities of warm weather. Black net spangled with steel and made up over white is as serviceable as any single item of the summer girl's wardrobe.


Blue spotted net made up over white net supplies an exceedingly dainty little dress, with waist cut in baby fashion, straps of lace across the shoulders and wreath of deep red roses around the skirt. If this gives too much color, a spray only of the flowers may be worn, on the left shoulder. A trifle more dressy than this is made of white point esprit peppered with silver spangles and made up over a single layer of pale green chiffon.

STRIKE AND ITS SIZE IS REDUCED—STRIKERS
HUNTING EVERYWHERE FOR MEN.

On the second day of the strike at "The Sun"
the newspaper is still found in a badly
grip state. The boatload of printers who, it was
said, had been hired in Philadelphia did not
materialize to any extent in The Sun's com-
ming room last night. The invading army of
printers apparently reached this city from the
Jersey City all right, but the emissaries of the
union soon converted them over to the doc-
trine of unionism, and they did not go to The
Sun's office.

They had spent the night on the steamboat En-
deavor, which was anchored off Bay Ridge. At
early hour the Endeavor steamed up to Pier
North River, where its passengers were
landed. In the mean time the strikers' union
engaged the tug Elkins which had followed
the Endeavor up from her anchorage of the
night before. The printers on the Endeavor,
at landing, were taken to the Sixth-Ave. ele-
vated railroad at South Ferry, and rushed up
Portland-st. The strikers mingled freely with
them on the trip and so successful were in
the exercise of their persuasive power, that
the majority of the visitors made their way
to the headquarters of Typographical Union.
It was said that out of the one hundred
odd men only nine reached the office of
the union, and the majority of them were sent
to their homes in the course of the day.

Troubles also beset The Sun as the
compositional compositors who usually set the type
for the afternoon and evening editions also went
strike yesterday, and it was impossible to
make an edition of the paper until con-
veniently late hour. All the afternoon editions
were confined to four pages only, and much of
the matter they contained was reprint and that
had been up on the galleys to be used
in emergencies.

HELP FROM ANOTHER OFFICE.

Some assistance was sought last night by
the management. It was declared that the
Evening Post, which is known as a non-union
paper, had stepped into the breach and
rendered its services to The Sun's Printing and
Publishing Company in getting out this morn-
ing's edition. The Wall Street page and all
tabulated matter was set on the Linotype
machines in "The Evening Post" office. The
newly set type were then taken to The Sun
via The Sun's delivery wagons which were
guarded by policemen in citizens' clothes.

At a corner of The Sun, it was said that
there was nothing new in the situation. It
was also said that the work of getting out
the paper was moving along smoothly.

John J. Delaney, the newly elected president
of Typographical Union No. 6, was an extremely
busy man yesterday and he was seen with the
Executive Committee of the organization and
a large force of volunteers.

At 8 o'clock last night President Delaney
gave out the following statement:

We are more than satisfied with the situa-
tion. Reports received from all over the
country prove that The Sun is making every
effort to secure men by all kinds of promises,
but the members of the International Union are
alert everywhere, and have found little difficulty
in rendering the work of The Sun impossible.
Indignation is expressed by fair-minded
men everywhere at the alleged low wages of
The Sun, relative to the wages paid. The
wages offered by The Sun range from $8 to
$9 a week less than the union newspaper scale
in New-York.

MR. JAFFAN'S COURSE CRITICISED.

Mr. Jaffan in the morning newspapers also
strongly denies any knowledge of Charles Will-
iam Edwards, of the steamboat Endeavor, or of
the circulars which the representatives of the
union presented to Mr. Paddock on Saturday
evening and requested affirmation or denial
of their authenticity. At the time Mr. Jaffan
made this denial the Endeavor was anchored off
Bay Ridge and Mr. Edwards had left the steam-
boat in a rowboat and was then receiving mis-
tructions near Pier North River, with his men,
all in possession of one of the circulars which
the representatives of the union submitted to
Mr. Paddock on Saturday evening.

Concerning the other circular, the one which
told the employees of The Sun that their posi-
tions were to be made vacant and dated August
and signed by The Sun Printing and Publishing
Association, had been posted up by men
in various parts of the boat.

When the situation was explained to the men
by the union's representatives, they met them
on the wharf although they were guarded by
the police. All but nine of them left Mr. Edwards
and accompanied us to the headquarters of
the union. The nine were taken directly to the
Sun office. An hour later five of the nine came
out leaving only four as net result of the ex-
pedition.

"Our organization was never so perfect, our
members are enthusiastic and we cannot be
driven."

The latest reports last night were that about
twenty-five hands were working in The Sun
comprising rooms, among them being several
typographical staff who had learned to stick type
in bygone days. The reporter found no
type was permitted to make more space than

Secretary Ranecoff, of the State Board of Med-
iation and Arbitration, had conferences with both
Typographical Union No. 6 and The Sun rep-
resentatives, but nothing came of it.
President Delaney of Big Six and Dame
Harris, president of the State Workingmen's
Federation, had a conference with both,
nothing regarding it was given out to the
press. The State Workingmen's Federation
represents about one hundred thousand
men and is a branch of the American Fed-
eration of Labor. The latter body, it was said,

against The Sun.

"Every time we have a celebrity with us," said the chief clerk at one of the leading hotels, "I am certain to be deluged with autograph albums. They are left by people who calmly request me to waylay the notable and get his or her signature, preceded if possible by some neat and appropriate sentiment, verse preferred. As a rule, no explanation is necessary and all I have to do is to hand over the little books.
